catalog_quote: Fore has only one phonemic suprasegmental feature: pitch-accent, to which I shall refer simply as 'accent'. As in a stress system, the unit of accent placement is the syllable, even though the main diagnostic feature of Fore accent is pitch. An accented syllable incurs higher pitch, which may be either level or falling. ... Each morpheme has its own underlying accent patterning. The surface realisation of accent in words results from the combination of these underlying patterns. [p.20] There are two components to a morpheme's underlying accent. Firstly, a morpheme may be accented on one of its syllable nuclei, or it may be completely unaccented. Two accents on a single morpheme occur, but never on adjacent syllables. Secondly, a morpheme may induce an accent on a following syllable ... This induced accent may be the sole distinguishing factor between otherwise homophonous forms ... [p.2…
sweep_summary: Fore (fore1270, catalog: tonal/pitch accent, Scott 1978). Four works with stress in the title = three works: (1)+(2) Pike & Scott 1963 ZPSK/STUF 16:179-189, the dedicated pitch accent analysis, duplicated in Glottolog; paywalled at De Gruyter (DOI 10.1524/stuf.1963.16.14.179), online with a university library loginvia the Harvard library catalogue; Scott 1978 fn.28/p.22 summarise it (stress-type system cued by pitch not intensity) — medium priority, would deepen evidence, not change coding. (3) Scott 1990 'A reanalysis of Fore accent', La Trobe WP in Linguistics 3:139-150, not in our bibliography and not obtainable today (SIL PNG archive id 48692 down; no Crossref/OA record found) — HIGH priority: same analyst's later reanalysis is the one item that could refine or change the classification. (4) Pilch 1970 Kivung 3(2):133-142, held by the project and read (scanned): secondary argument that the Fore 'accent' is distinctive word-stress realised by pitch; no placement data; Scott 1978 p.22 rebuts his 'three patterns' claim — refines label only. Best statement read remains the deciding source itself (Scott 1978 §2.31.1 pp.19-20, verbatim in held text); catalog's classification confirmed, nothing supersedes it. archive.

new_statements.reading: This is the catalog's own deciding source, re-read verbatim in the copy we hold: Fore has lexically specified pitch accent (per-morpheme underlying accent, including unaccented and post-accenting morphemes), with surface restraints (max two adjacent accents; no word-initial adjacent accents except disyllables in isolation), no weight or edge rule, and 'No contrastive intonation patterns occur' (p. 23). Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title supersedes it: the only newly read item, Pilch 1970, is a secondary terminological argument (call it distinctive word-stress realised by pitch) that Scott 1978 p. 22 already addresses; the dedicated primary analysis (Pike & Scott 1963) is paywalled and Scott's own 1990 'reanalysis' could not be obtained.

There is also some contrast in intensity, particularly on phrase-final syllables. ... we analysed this system in Fore as one of contrastive 'pitch- accent', in which syllables were seen to be either prominent ('accented') or not. new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same data as the catalog's deciding source (Scott 1978 §2.31, 'pitch accent' with the syllable as the unit of accent placement and the constraints 'no more than two adjacent accents' / 'no word-initial adjacent accents'), but the TYPE is changed: Scott 1990 argues the system is morpheme-level tone melodies with floating tones on an autosegmental tier, explicitly rejecting analyses that assign accents or tones to individual syllables underlyingly, and derives the 1978 constraints from melody mapping instead. It agrees with the catalog on everything a stress catalog needs (prominence is lexically specified, pitch-based, not intensity-based, no fixed or weight-driven stress positi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Scott replaces his own 1978 syllable-based 'pitch accent' analysis with an autosegmental word-tone analysis: each morpheme carries an underlying tone melody (monosyllables L, H, LH, HL; disyllables L, H, LH, HL, LHL, HLH), the last tone of which is a 'floating' tone that replaces the first tone of the following morpheme (the old 'induced accent'); melodies map one tone per syllable (no contrastive contours), spreading L in preference to H, and adjacent H tones merge. This yields exactly the attested 4 patterns on disyllables and 6 on trisyllables and reduces the 11 four-syllable patterns of Scott 1978 to 8. Prominence is lexical and pitch-based; intensity is not the basic correlate; there is no positional (edge- or weight-based) stress rule. Referent/object prefixes and the sentence-final Indicative suffix are toneless; Interrogative and Imperative mood suffixes carry their own H.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none discussed (no stress tiers; H tones described as 'peaks of prominence or pitch targets', §4 PDF p.8)
new_statements.exceptions: §5 'Aberrations': inalienable-possession and object prefixes are toneless and take tone from the root rather than inducing it; the citation Indicative suffix -e is toneless; Interrogative -o and Imperative carry an H that overrides floating tones (possibly a general non-statement sentence-end H); the vowel-less perfect -nt carries a floating H; four of the 1978 four-syllable contrasts (LLHH vs HLLH, LLHL vs HLHL-type, LHHL vs LHLL, HLHH) are withdrawn as not genuinely contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Scott's data are Fore as described in Scott 1978/1980 (his fieldwork base was the Northern/Central Fore area; the 1990 paper does not name a dialect and treats 'Fore' as one system, c. 20,000 speakers).

readall_conflicts: Scott 1978 (the catalog's source, with Pike & Scott 1963) labels Fore prominence 'pitch accent' assigned per syllable with two surface constraints; Scott 1990, the same author's later reanalysis now read in full, recasts it as a restricted word-tone system (per-morpheme melodies L/H/LH/HL/LHL/HLH plus a floating tone, L-spreading, H-merger) and states that Fore 'does not easily fit a theory which assigns accents or tones to individual syllables underlyingly'. The disagreement is one of analysis type (syllable-linked accent vs autosegmental morpheme tone), not of facts: both say prominence is lexical and realised by pitch, intensity is secondary (some phrase-final intensity contrast only), and neither gives any positional or weight-based word-stress rule. Pilch 1970 (already held by the project) is a third terminological position (call it distinctive word-stress realised by pitch). Nicholson & Nicholson 1962, cited in Scott 1990, treat it as tone with slightly different pattern inventories.

sources.quote: 'Accent, marked by an acute over the vowel (or over the first vowel of a diphthong), is included throughout for purposes of reference, though left unwritten in local Fore publications. Fore phonology is presented in detail by Nicholson and Nicholson (1962), and again by Scott (1978). Analysis of accent is given by Pike and Scott (1963), concerning which Pilch (1970) has made some remarks.' Entries carry lexically placed accent marks (N/S dialect forms).
sources.note: Accent-marked lexicon by the same author; confirms accent is lexically specified per entry (downloaded now).

sources.quote: Secondary/theoretical, no new data: 'Fore words are characterized by different pitch patterns... There are minimal pairs which differ audibly by pitch only. Pike and Scott hesitate whether to categorize these pitch patterns as tone or stress... What Pike-Scott call accent turns out to be stress manifested by phonetic parameters other than loudness' ... 'if we categorize the Fore accent as stress, then Fore is a language with distinctive word-stress'. Scott 1978 p.22 rebuts Pilch's 'exactly three pitch patterns' claim as misleading.
